At the highest power setting of 600 W, total electrical consumption represented 0.25 percent of engine output, satisfying the target of consuming less than one percent of engine power. The stronger response observed at higher engine speeds was attributed to improved in-cylinder fuel– air mixing and shorter residence times, conditions under which plasma-generated hydrogen and acetylene more effectively enhance oxidation chemistry. These reactive species are believed to accelerate the breakdown of unburned methane and improve combustion completeness, particularly in engines operating with lean or rapidly mixed charge conditions. Combustion analysis revealed measurable changes in both the heat-release rate (HRR) and cylinder-pressure behavior during plasma-assisted operation. Figure 20 presents the average HRR profiles as a function of crank angle. Compared to baseline operation, the plasma-activated fuel exhibited a slightly delayed main combustion phase and a lower peak HRR. This outcome reflects the reduced carbon content and lower total heating value of the plasma-reformed fuel, which offsets the higher peak pressures typically associated with hydrogen addition. The partial conversion of methane to hydrogen, acetylene, and short-chain hydrocarbons removes a portion of the carbon energy, resulting in a smaller total heat release. Simultaneously, hydrogen and intermediate species promote faster oxidation kinetics, producing a more spatially uniform flame. The combined effect is a smoother, more evenly distributed combustion process that minimizes localized hot spots and reduces the potential for incomplete oxidation. The plasma cases show a slight delay and lower peak HRR relative to baseline operation, consistent with reduced carbon content in the reformate and a smoother, more uniform burn profile. Cycle-resolved analysis of the indicated mean effective pressure (IMEP) demonstrated that combustion stability remained well within acceptable limits during plasma-assisted operation. Figure 21 shows normalized IMEP distributions for cylinders two through six across plasma duty cycles of 50%, 75%, and 100%. The data indicate consistent combustion phasing and minimal variability, with no evidence of cycle-to-cycle instability or misfire events. These findings confirm that plasma enrichment did not disturb engine balance or control system operation and support that the fuel’s total heating value is being reduced (reduced IMEP) as the plasma duty cycle increases.
